20204-the-storm-cloud-of-the-nineteenth-:
John Ruskin gave The Storm-Cloud of the Nineteenth Century as two lectures in 1884. The first lecture is printed much as he gave it on February 4. He repeated it on February 11 with several passages enlarged. Its last part changed to suit a wider public interest then.

Ruskin saw a new, dark haze fouling skies he had known as bright. He blamed coal smoke and industry for that grim storm-cloud. The lectures mix sharp sky watching with moral anger at pollution. Readers get an early, vivid warning on air and industry from a master critic.
20956-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-iv:
God rest you merry, gentlemen, rings out in In the Yule-Log Glow, Book Four, from 1891. The carol's tidings of comfort and joy set the volume's Christmas key. Harrison Weir and others gathered tales to match that glow of hearth and hymn.

Stories, poems, and carols for the season fill book four of this holiday set. Snow, bells, feasts, and kindly deeds warm its pages in turn. Victorian Christmas books fed a new cult of the festive home. This one shows the trade at its coziest, made to be read aloud while the yule log burned low.
21671-army-boys-on-the-firing-line-or-ho:
Homer Randall sends his Army Boys against the German drive in Army Boys on the Firing Line, copyrighted in 1919. Frank and Tom Bradford trade fire with raiders who rush their line. The last rush, Tom jokes, went back in a bigger hurry than it came.

Front pictures show Frank hurling his revolver in a sentry's face. Chapters promise capture, a midnight swim, a drugged detachment, and a mined bridge. Nick Rabig turns up again as the tale's villain. Randall's series, begun with Army Boys in France, gave American boys a brisk, patriotic tale of the Great War's last year.
21775-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
British and Irish prose from 1672 to 1800 fills this fourth volume of The Best of the World's Classics, published in 1909. Henry Cabot Lodge served as editor-in-chief, with Francis W. Halsey beside him. The volume is the second of two covering Great Britain and Ireland. Portraits of Johnson, Goldsmith, Pope, and Gibbon front the book.

Inside, readers meet Sir Richard Steele in pieces from The Guardian, The Spectator, and The Tatler, including Sir Roger and the Widow. Lord Bolingbroke follows, writing on the shortness of life and the study of history. Each author comes with a short life and notes. The set aimed to put the world's best prose, briefly framed, into ordinary homes.
22254-the-substance-of-a-journal-during-:
John West, a Church of England chaplain, kept a journal at the Red River Colony in the years 1820 to 1823. West was the Hudson's Bay Company's first Protestant chaplain in the Northwest. His Substance of a Journal appeared as missionary interest in British North America was rising. He writes of a day when distant parts of the earth were opening to missionary labour, and British sympathy with them.

West describes Lord Selkirk's settlers, the fur trade, Indigenous peoples, and brutal winters. He founded a school and a church on the Red River, in what is now Manitoba. The journal is a founding document of western Canada.
22343-the-wedding-ring-a-series-of-disco:
T. De Witt Talmage preached The Wedding Ring, a series of discourses for husbands and wives, in 1896. Talmage was a famous American preacher of his day. His talks take marriage cases straight from Scripture.

One discourse opens with Samson, the giant of the Bible. Samson asks his parents to consent to a marriage they judge unfit. He was wise, Talmage says, to ask their counsel. He was not wise in rejecting it once given. From such stories the sermons draw rules for home life. Readers get Victorian marriage teaching in a preacher's strong, plain, and confident voice.
a-theological-political-treatise-part-iv:
Baruch Spinoza closes his Theologico-Political Treatise with part four, chapters sixteen to twenty, on the state and the rights of rulers and subjects. He begins with nature, where right reaches as far as power does. From there he asks how people pass from that rough state into civil order.

The chapters define civil right and wrong, treaties, and treason, then test his ideas against the old Hebrew republic under Moses and after. Spinoza argues that no one can give up all his rights to a ruler, and that a state stays safest when people may think and speak freely. The part ends his case for free thought.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-iv:
In 1865 Barbier de Meynard issued the fourth tome of Les Prairies d'Or, his French version of the Muruj al-Dhahab. Al-Masudi composed the Meadows of Gold in the tenth century after years of travel through the Islamic world and beyond. The Société Asiatique set runs to nine tomes in all.

Across the work, history and geography walk hand in hand. The lands of the earth come with their kings, faiths, customs, and marvels. Then the annals of Islam run down to the author's lifetime. Al-Masudi quotes poets, sailors, and court scholars with equal delight. Meynard's French, aided by Pavet de Courteille, became the standard Masudi for Europe. Tome four keeps the long narrative moving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-iv: This 1913 reference article on Boniface IV — the pope of the Pantheon's gift. Thomas Oestereich honors his long reign. He turned the Pantheon into a church. The monks of Monte Cassino knew him. The pope who hallowed the Pantheon. His Santa Maria ad Martyres is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clement-xiv: This 1913 reference piece on Clement XIV — the pope of the suppression. Joseph Wilhelm weighs his fateful brief. He dissolved the Society of Jesus. The Bourbon courts forced his hand. The pope of the Dominus ac Redemptor. His Ganganelli name was the conclave's choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-iv: This 1913 reference piece on Henry IV — the Bourbon king. Georges Goyau unfolds his famous conversion. Paris was worth the holy Mass. The realm bless the merry name. The founder of the Bourbon line. His 1610 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-xiv: A 1913 entry on Louis XIV — the Sun King. Georges Goyau unfolds his seventy-two years. He crowned the Bourbon glory. Europe knew the splendid name. The seventeenth century told his tale. His 1715 death is famed. His 1643 reign is famed. His 1643 Versailles glory is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nerses-i-iv: The Nerses were the great catholicoi of Armenia, the patriarchs who guided the nation's church through its formative centuries. This entry covers the four most famous, their reforms, and their legacy. The fathers of the Armenian Church: Nerses the Great founded its hospitals and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-iv: Otto IV was the Welf emperor who quarreled with Innocent III and fell at Bouvines. This entry covers his reign, his excommunication, and his ruin. The emperor the pope unmade: his crushing defeat at Bouvines ended the Welfs' imperial dream.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-i: Adrian IV was the only English pope, the Hertfordshire boy who crowned emperors. This entry traces his pontificate, his bull Laudabiliter, and his times. The Englishman on Peter's throne: his fateful Ireland grant shaped all the subsequent history of Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-alexande: Alexander IV was the pope of the Hohenstaufen's fall and the Mongol embassies. This entry traces his pontificate, his trials, and his letters. The pope of the dying empire: his brave friars preached the perilous Mongol mission to the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-anastasi: Anastasius IV was the aged pope of the 1150s who crowned no emperor. This entry traces his brief pontificate, his letters, and his times. The octogenarian of the twelfth century: his brief reign soothed troubled, aging Rome for a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict: Benedict IV was the pope who crowned Louis the Blind in 901. This entry notes his pontificate, his synods, and the scant records. The pope of the fading Carolingians: his stern synods condemned the grasping simoniacs of Italy and beyond.

Benedict XIV was the learned Lambertini, the Enlightenment's favorite pope. This entry traces his pontificate, his scholarship, and his wit. The scholar on Peter's throne: his sparkling wit charmed the skeptical philosophes of all enlightened Europe with true effortless ease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin: Celestine IV was the pope whose reign lasted sixteen days in 1241. This entry notes his election in the conclave's prison and his swift death. The pope of the sequestered conclave: his sudden death stalled the long papal election for years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-: Clement IV was the French pope who crowned Charles of Anjou. This entry traces his pontificate, his crusade plans, and his austerity. The lawyer of the Angevin cause: his wise letters guided the last crusade of Saint Louis to Tunis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-eugene-i: Eugene IV was the pope of the Council of Florence and the Greek reunion. This entry traces his pontificate, his council, and his wars. The pope of Laetentur Caeli: his great council reunited East and West briefly in 1439's decree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-felix-iv: Felix IV was the pope of Theodoric's Ostrogothic Italy. This entry traces his pontificate, his churches, and his semi-Arian past. The pope of the Gothic peace: his noble basilicas graced old Ravenna's golden age of sacred art and mosaic work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-: Gregory IV was the pope of the Carolingian empire's civil wars. This entry notes his pontificate, his mediations, and the scant records. The peacemaker of the Frankish brothers: his Field of Lies betrayal shamed him forever in song and story.

Gregory XIV was the Sfondrati pope of the early 1590s. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his French intervention, and the scant records. A quiet name of the Counter-Reformation: his few months backed the Catholic League in warring France with gold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-honorius: Honorius IV was the aged Savelli pope of the mid-1280s. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his Sicilian wars, and the scant records. The old Roman of the Vespers' aftermath: his brief reign steadied troubled Rome awhile in fragile peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent: Innocent IV was the pope who deposed Frederick II at Lyons. This entry traces his pontificate, his council, and his long war. The lawyer who humbled an emperor: his Lyons council deposed proud Frederick in 1245's hot summer session at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-iv: John IV was the Dalmatian pope who ransomed captives from the Slavs. This entry traces his pontificate, his charity, and his orthodoxy. The pope of the redeemed slaves: his papal gold freed the wretched captives in ravaged Dalmatia itself in 641.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xiv: John XIV was the pope starved to death in the Castel Sant'Angelo. This entry traces his brief pontificate, his imprisonment, and his murder. The martyr of the Crescentii: his cruel starvation shamed all of Christian Rome forevermore in that dark 984.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-martin-i: Martin IV was the French pope of the Sicilian Vespers' fury. This entry traces his pontificate, his Angevin loyalty, and Dante's judgment. The pope Dante set among the gluttons: his beloved Lake Bolsena eels were famous in Dante's immortal verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas: Nicholas IV was the first Franciscan pope, patron of missions to the Mongols. This entry traces his pontificate, his friars, and his diplomacy. The Minorite on the throne: his brave friars reached the Great Khan's distant court in far Cathay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-iv: Paul IV was the terrible Carafa pope of the Inquisition's rigors. This entry traces his pontificate, his reforms, and his hatreds. The scourge of the Roman Jews: his cruel ghetto walled the Jewish quarter of Rome in 1555's hot July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-iv: Pius IV was the Medici pope who concluded the Council of Trent. This entry traces his pontificate, his council, and his reforms. The closer of Trent: his solemn decrees sealed the great council of Trent forever in 1563's cold December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-le: Leo IV was the pope who built the Leonine Wall against the Saracens. This entry traces his pontificate, his walls, and his victory at Ostia. The defender of Rome: his massive walls stand to this very day in Rome itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sergius-: Sergius IV was the pope of 1009 whose brief reign left little trace. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A quiet name of the millennium's turn: his months passed in peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sixtus-i: Sixtus IV was the della Rovere pope who built the Sistine Chapel. This entry traces his pontificate, his nepotism, and his Rome. The pope of the chapel's name: his grasping nephews ruled all of Renaissance Rome openly and proudly in power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-: Stephen III was the pope of the Lombard wars' climax and Desiderius's fall. This entry traces his pontificate, his trials, and his times. The pope of the Franks' deliverance: his desperate appeal brought young Charlemagne south in 773's bright autumn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-iv: Urban IV was the pope who instituted Corpus Christi. This entry traces his pontificate, his feast, and his French wars. The pope of the Blessed Sacrament's feast: his famous bull founded Corpus Christi's feast in 1264's bright August days at Orvieto.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-iv: Raymond IV of Toulouse was the great count of the First Crusade. This entry traces his campaigns, his piety, and his death. The crusader of Provence: his proud banner led the crusading host to Jerusalem's holy walls in 1099's July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-canute-iv: St. Canute IV was the martyr king of Denmark. This entry traces his Odense, his church, and his cult. The saint of the Danish throne: his martyr's blood sealed Odense in the 1086 of the revolt in the church of St. Alban.
doe-osti-2999156-radiation-characterizat: Godiva IV environments got characterized, and this DOE summary covers the critical assembly radiation. The pages detail the in-core and 1m findings. The health physicists get their numbers. The assembly was Godiva IV. The summary was radiation. The physicists got numbers.
doe-osti-3013857-engineered-barrier-syst: SNL barriers got FY25-researched, and this DOE text covers engineered system activities. The pages detail the findings. The waste folks get their data. The lab was Sandia. The data were waste. The report was FY25. The activities were research.
doe-osti-3017118-the-fastrshwfs-project-: FastrSHWFS got motivation-analyzed, and this DOE project covers test results. The pages detail the development findings. The engineers get their data. The results were test. The data were engineer. The analysis was motivation. The project was FastrSHWFS. The results were analysis.
doe-osti-3023834-methodology-for-determi: Odd-shaped buildings getting their plane-crash math got the DOE area method, and this text sizes the impact zone. The pages detail the facility results. The engineers get their data. The method was effective area. The zone was impact.
doe-osti-3220611-design-of-multi-engine-: Freight locomotives got multi-engine-designed, and this DOE text covers the design. The pages detail the findings. The transport folks get their data. The design was multi-engine. The data were transport. The freight were locomotive. The engine were multi.
doe-osti-3376058-a-simulation-resource-t: Fusion concepts got simulation-teamed, and this DOE text covers innovative resources. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The team was resource. The data were physicist. The fusion were concepts. The innovative were resources. The physicists were data.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: Maxwell Lehman, civil service leader, is the subject named in this pre-assassination-era declassified US government file. The Internet Archive's record offers the title alone - no date, no context. No public text found. A name from the files, kept on record.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-iv:
Book Four of Lytton's Leila opens inside a besieged castle. News breaks in on Leila's calm prayers and holy anxieties. Every inhabitant of the castle feels the fearful interest of that news.

The siege of Granada now touches daily life directly. Moors and Christians prepare for the struggle's hardest phase. Leila's love and faith face their sharpest tests yet. Lytton slows the war to show one woman's inner battle. The fourth book readies readers for the great battle ahead. Almamen the enchanter gives the tale a magical thread. Granada's palace scenes mix splendor with quiet dread.
nasa-tm-19670028225-stratospheric-temper:
Guenter Warnecke and Andrew W. McCulloch, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, presented this paper in London, England, in July 1967. The meeting was the tenth plenary session of COSPAR, the international space research committee. Their subject is temperature patterns in the stratosphere, drawn from measurements by the Nimbus II weather satellite.

The satellite's infrared radiometer imaged the Earth in a carbon dioxide absorption band that senses stratospheric temperature, alongside a clear window channel. Because clouds contaminate the picture, one section treats the elimination of cloud influence. The paper then presents stratospheric temperature distribution maps for four days in May, June, and July 1966. A typical image shows the temperature pattern running from high values over the Arctic down to low values far in the southern latitudes. The cloud pattern appears superimposed, from the window channel.
nasa-tm-19700029986-an-analytical-develo:
Richard W. Barbieri of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1970. It develops, in math form, how two close satellites move in relation to each other. Both satellites circle a planet that is not a perfect sphere, but slightly flattened at the poles.

The study describes the sideways relative motion of satellites flying only a few kilometres apart. That gap is tiny beside their distance from the planet's center, which the paper takes as far larger. The work supported studies of orbiting long baseline interferometry, including the proposed Radio Astronomy Explorer pair. Equations came from a Lagrangian formulation, with the satellites' pull on each other left out.
object-lessons-on-the-human-body-a-trans:
Sarah F. Buckelew wrote Object Lessons on the Human Body from lessons given in a New York primary school. The subtitle names the primary department of School No. 49, in New York City. Parker P. Simmons issued this revised pupils' edition in 1904. It belongs to a series called Practical Work in the School Room.

Her note to the pupil calls the body the house you live in. Children must learn to guard that house from two great enemies, alcohol and nicotine. She warns them not to talk parrot fashion, saying words the mind does not grasp. Knowledge must be paid for with attention, she adds, through one's own eyes and ears. Nobody else can pay that price.
poems-vol-iv:
Hattie Howard published the fourth volume of her Poems in Hartford in 1904, from the Case, Lockwood and Brainard press. Howard was a Connecticut writer of stories and verse with titles such as Poverty versus Pauperism, Our Girls, and Keeping a Secret to her name. The volume opens with press notices of a former volume, quoted at length, praising her poems of sentiment as natural, spontaneous, direct, and free from ambitious pretense.

The reviewers stress the book's sunny, hopeful spirit, welcome in a time of morbid expression, and its hearty, wholesome human feeling, sometimes overflowing into downright fun. An illustration shows her brother Harry Howard, a student, with a motto about the pure in heart. Howard wrote for the home circle rather than the academy, and volume four, arriving after three earlier volumes, testifies to a loyal local readership for cheerful, tender, plain-spoken verse.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-louis-:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Louis XIV draws its extracts from the memoirs of the Duchesse d'Orléans. Her letters and recollections report the Sun King's court from within. Prepared by David Widger, the selection runs in alphabetical order, one pointed sentence at a time.

A pious Capuchin explains a dream, the Queen gets only the rinsings of the glass, and duplicity passes for wit while frankness counts as folly. The Duchess mocks high head-dresses, horrid swearing, and excessive bathing. She wonders aloud whether the King believes in the existence of a God at all. The volume gains its tart, gossipy flavor from such lines.
the-child-and-childhood-in-folk-thought-:
Alexander Francis Chamberlain, M.A., Ph.D., studies the child in folk thought in this book, grown from lectures he gave at Clark University's summer school in 1894. Its full title promises studies of what children do and how they shape life among early peoples, with matches and survivals in modern culture. He dedicates the work to his father and mother, with a verse from Goethe.

In his prefatory note Chamberlain ties the book to the child-study movement then drawing teachers and parents. His aim is to mark the chief things children do among primitive peoples, then trace how those acts live on in today's social forms and culture movements. The point of view, he insists, stays with the child and what the child has done in all ages and among all races. Readers get an early work of anthropology that treats children's play and custom as serious evidence.
the-tent-on-the-beach-and-other-poems-pa:
John Greenleaf Whittier's Tent on the Beach gathers narrative poems around a poetical picnic on the New Hampshire coast. His prelude names his two companions, Fields the lettered magnate and Taylor the free cosmopolite, without quite naming them. He pictures the Hampton River winding through salt-meadows near the tent. Great Boar's Head bluff stands northward, and Newburyport lifts its steeples to the south.

The contents promise legends told in the tent: The Wreck of Rivermouth, The Changeling, The Maids of Attitash, The Palatine, and Abraham Davenport. Whittier's opening verse calls his plot simple, old fancies from boyhood warmed into life again. Readers who like New England legend in ballad form will find the whole programme laid out invitingly.
the-traveling-engineers-association-to-i:
The Traveling Engineers' Association issued its examination questions and answers for firemen seeking promotion, copyrighted by W. O. Thompson in 1911 and revised in January 1919. The preface explains railroad policy: companies employ firemen who will in time become competent engineers. A candidate needs at least a common school education, good habits, sound judgment, and good physical condition. Advancement comes to men conscientious in duty who study in their leisure hours.

The question code tests how far a fireman has progressed, year by year, and guides what he must know both as fireman and as future engineer. This practical manual preserves the world of steam railroading from inside the cab. Readers meet the era's faith in self-improvement, where a workingman's promotion depended on mastering boilers, brakes, and rules through printed questions.
